### You Are Here

The cartographer’s shop appeared only when it rained.

It stood between the bakery and the shuttered cinema, in a gap too narrow for a door, and smelled of pencil shavings, ink, and wet wool. The sign said:

**E. VALE**  
**MAPS OF ROADS, RIVERS, AND OTHER WAYS HOME**

By day, Elena Vale drew ordinary maps: property lines, footpaths, the changing mouth of the river. After midnight, people came with stranger requests. A road to the house as it had sounded before the argument. The coastline of a life in which a letter had arrived on time. Once, a trumpet player asked for a map of the silence after his final note.

Elena never promised return. She only drew the country around an absence.

Her price was not money, but one true sentence.

The old man arrived one October night carrying a leather notebook against his chest. Water shone on his shoulders.

“I need a road back to my wife,” he said.

Elena was cleaning a nib. “Is she dead?”

“No.”

“Then I can’t help you.”

“She’s alive. She’s in a room with yellow curtains. She likes the curtains. She hates the soup. Most mornings she doesn’t know my name.”

He opened the notebook. Its pages were crowded with dates.

Arthur and Clare, married 1961. Arthur and Clare, two daughters. Arthur and Clare, the house on Bell Street, the dog with one ear, the holiday in Wales where it rained so hard they gave up sightseeing and stayed in bed.

“I’ve been keeping the facts,” he said.

“And?”

“And they aren’t working.”

Elena pulled a sheet of paper toward her.

“Tell me about the last place you were certain you were together.”

He thought for a long time.

“A kitchen,” he said at last. “Nineteen sixty-three. There was a storm. The roof leaked into a blue bowl, and the radio kept losing the station. Clare took off her wet socks and danced in her bare feet. I was pretending to fix the wireless, but really I was watching her.”

“What song?”

“I don’t remember.”

“What were you wearing?”

“I don’t remember.”

“What did she say?”

He closed his eyes.

“She said, ‘Arthur, stop improving things and come here.’”

Elena began to draw.

She drew the kitchen at the edge of the paper, though there were no walls, only the blue bowl and four small marks for bare feet. She drew the road from Bell Street, the apricot tree that had died in the frost, the station where Clare had once left him behind as a joke and he had not found it funny. Around these things she drew hills, rivers, borders.

At the center she left a white space.

Arthur frowned. “You haven’t finished.”

“That part is hers. I won’t draw it for her.”

“Then how do I get there?”

“You don’t.”

He stood so abruptly that his chair scraped the floor.

Elena capped her ink. “You asked for a road back. There isn’t one. This is a map of where you’ve been standing while you waited.”

He looked at the white space.

“What am I supposed to do with it?”

“Leave the notebook at home. Go sit at the edge.”

“My fee,” he said bitterly. “You charge a true sentence.”

“Yes.”

His hand tightened on the notebook.

“I keep asking her questions I know she can’t answer,” he said. “Because if she gets one right, I think I can bear the rest.”

Elena gave him the map.

Three weeks later, he returned.

“Your map is useless,” he said.

“Yes.”

He stared at her, then laughed once, unwillingly.

He sat down.

“I left the notebook at home. Clare was in the garden, putting stones in the birdbath. The nurse kept taking them out, and Clare kept putting them back. I asked if I could help. She said I could, provided I didn’t arrange them.”

“Did you?”

“For nearly an hour. She called me Tom once. I didn’t correct her. A wren came down to drink, and she grabbed my sleeve. Not my hand. My sleeve. Like I was a post.”

He looked at his hands.

“It wasn’t like before.”

“No.”

“I kept waiting for it to be.”

Elena said nothing.

“Then I stopped,” he said. “And there she was. Not my Clare from the kitchen. Not the one who knew all the facts. But not no one.”

The rain softened against the windows.

Before leaving, Arthur said, “I’m still lonely.”

“Yes,” Elena said.

He nodded, as if she had finally drawn something accurately.

After he had gone, Elena took down the blank sheet that had hung above her desk for years. She had been saving it, she realized, for some country whose absence she could name.

Instead she drew the bakery. The cinema with its broken letters. The narrow shop, the river, the road leading uphill out of town. Nothing missing. Nothing restored.

At the center she marked a point no larger than a pinprick.

**HERE.**

Then she unlocked the door and stepped outside.

The rain had stopped. Without making any fuss about it, the street was there.
